identification.title: God the Uncreated One (King Forevermore)
identification.notes: Words and music by Aaron Keyes and Pete James. CCLI 7057478. Copyright 2016 to 10000 Fathers, Common Hymnal Publishing, Thankyou Music and Getty Music Hymns and Songs. Credited to Aaron Keyes as the artist whose recording carried it into congregational use.

claims.structuralNotes: Four verses, each closing on a refrain with one word changed at the front ('He is King', 'Crown Him King', 'Reign as King'), resolving on an outro of 'King of kings forever'. Verses 1-3 speak about God in the third person; verse 4 turns to direct address. Sequence: creation, God's rule over history, the cross and resurrection, eternal reign.

claims.claim: God is uncreated — the source of everything, deriving his being from nothing outside himself.
claims.subject: Aseity

claims.claim: God is the origin of salvation, not merely its announcer.
claims.subject: Soteriology

claims.claim: God set the stars in place; the image is domestic and deliberate.
claims.subject: Creation

claims.claim: God's attention extends to the smallest particulars of creation.
claims.subject: Omniscience

claims.claim: The God who orders the cosmos also knows each person inwardly.
claims.subject: Omniscience
claims.lyricExcerpt: Knows the heart of every man

claims.claim: God is the refuge and strength of his people.
claims.subject: Providence
claims.lyricExcerpt: God our fortress and our strength

claims.claim: God is a stable foundation that can be relied upon.
claims.subject: Providence
claims.lyricExcerpt: The Rock on which we can depend

claims.claim: God's majesty is without equal.
claims.subject: Doctrine of God

claims.claim: God does not change; he is the same self-existent God who named himself to Moses.
claims.subject: Immutability

claims.claim: Empires rise and collapse without affecting God's faithfulness.
claims.subject: Providence over history

claims.claim: God remains faithful through every upheaval.
claims.subject: Faithfulness of God

claims.claim: The almighty God is himself present in real human flesh.
claims.subject: Incarnation

claims.claim: Christ was betrayed — the passion narrative is named concretely.
claims.subject: Passion

claims.claim: The one pierced is the promised Prince of Peace.
claims.subject: Crucifixion

claims.claim: The crucified one was without sin.
claims.subject: Sinlessness of Christ

claims.claim: Christ died as a spotless sacrificial victim.
claims.subject: Substitutionary atonement

claims.claim: The Father raised him from death.
claims.subject: Resurrection

claims.claim: Christ reigns as king without end.
claims.subject: Kingship of Christ

claims.claim: God is eternal king and the source of grace.
claims.subject: Grace

claims.claim: The congregation crowns God with praise — the song turns to direct address.
claims.subject: Worship

claims.claim: God is thrice holy, echoing the seraphim's cry.
claims.subject: Holiness

theological.assessment: Unusually substantial for a contemporary song: aseity, creation, providence, immutability, incarnation, substitution, resurrection and reign, all orthodox and none muddled. Its limits are scope rather than accuracy — human sin is assumed and the Spirit is absent.

strengths.title: Opens on aseity
strengths.explanation: The first four words assert that God is uncreated — the source of everything, dependent on nothing. Congregational song almost never attempts this, and rarely without muddling it.
strengths.scriptureExcerpt: The God who made the world and everything in it… is not served by human hands, as though he needed anything.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Paul's argument in Athens is the hymn's opening claim exactly.

strengths.title: The incarnation stated without hedging
strengths.explanation: Not 'like God' or 'sent by God' — the mighty God himself, in mortal flesh. Four words carrying Chalcedon: full deity and real, dying humanity in one subject.
strengths.scriptureExcerpt: And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory.
strengths.scriptureRationale: John makes the same identification of the eternal Word with the man.

strengths.title: Sinlessness and sacrifice named together
strengths.explanation: The refrain pairs the sinless man with the spotless Lamb — stating both that Christ had no sin of his own and that he died as a sacrificial victim, which is what makes substitution coherent.
strengths.scriptureExcerpt: Ransomed… with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Peter supplies the exact register: an unblemished victim, and a ransom paid for others.

strengths.title: The resurrection is the Father's act
strengths.explanation: The hymn attributes the raising to the Father, which is the dominant New Testament idiom, and it does so in the same breath as the crucifixion rather than leaving the song at the cross.
strengths.scriptureExcerpt: God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Peter at Pentecost frames the resurrection the same way — as the Father's deliverance.

strengths.title: Immutability made pastoral
strengths.explanation: The unchanging God is set directly against the turnover of empires, so the comfort offered is that God will hold, not that circumstances will.
strengths.scriptureExcerpt: He changes times and seasons; he removes kings and sets up kings.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Political instability as an instance of God's rule, not evidence against it.

strengths.title: Transcendence and immanence in one breath
strengths.explanation: The first verse moves from hanging the stars to counting sand to knowing a human heart, as one continuous thought rather than two competing ideas.
strengths.lyricExcerpt: Knows the heart of every man
strengths.scriptureExcerpt: He determines the number of the stars; he gives to all of them their names.
strengths.scriptureRationale: The psalm makes the identical move from cosmic scale to personal attention.

strengths.title: Lands on the seraphim's cry
strengths.explanation: The final verse turns from description to address and closes on the threefold holy, placing the congregation in the posture of Isaiah 6 rather than merely talking about it.
strengths.scriptureExcerpt: Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!
strengths.scriptureRationale: The hymn ends where the seraphim begin.

communal.assessment: Built for a congregation: strophic, one repeated refrain shape, and a voice that moves from declaration to address. Length invites cutting. The vocal range was not independently verified — published in E and F, so check the tessitura locally before introducing it.
communal.vocalRangeNote: Not verified. Published arrangements appear in E and F; check locally and transpose without hesitation.
communal.repetitionAssessment: What repeats is 'forever' — the claim the hymn exists to make. Meaningful repetition, not padding.

strengths.title: One refrain, learned once
strengths.explanation: Only the opening word changes between verses — 'He is King', then 'Crown Him King', then 'Reign as King' — so a congregation effectively learns one refrain and can join from the first verse.

strengths.title: Turns to 'we' at the climax
strengths.explanation: Three verses declare who God is, then the fourth puts the act of crowning in the congregation's own mouth — corporate by grammar, not merely by convention.

strengths.title: The repeated word is the doctrine
strengths.explanation: 'Forever' is the claim, not filler, and it lets a congregation sing each verse's close without looking at a page.

concerns.title: Four verses invite cutting the best one
concerns.explanation: The verse most likely dropped for time is the third — incarnation, cross, resurrection — which is the one the hymn least survives without.

range.note: No chart was available to read the melody from. PraiseCharts lists F as the original key with an E arrangement, but does not state the pitches.

clarity.assessment: Clear despite the doctrinal density: concrete biblical imagery, contemporary diction, almost no archaism. Two small frictions worth a sentence of introduction the first time a congregation meets it.

strengths.title: A domestic picture for a cosmic act
strengths.explanation: Chandeliers make the hanging of the stars graspable without trivialising it, and the register is biblical — Isaiah stretches the heavens out like a curtain.
strengths.scriptureExcerpt: Who stretches out the heavens like a curtain, and spreads them like a tent to dwell in.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Scripture uses household imagery for cosmic acts in exactly this way.

strengths.title: One line carries two doctrines
strengths.explanation: Kingdoms rising and falling set against God's faithfulness puts providence and immutability into a phrase people take home.

strengths.title: Hymn weight without archaism
strengths.explanation: Traditional structure and contemporary vocabulary — 'the Rock on which we can depend' is plain speech doing doctrinal work, and needs no translation.
strengths.scriptureExcerpt: The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer, my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge.
strengths.scriptureRationale: The image arrives already carrying its biblical sense.

concerns.title: 'Uncreated' appears once and is never unpacked
concerns.explanation: The word does the heaviest theological work in the song, sits in the opening line, and never returns — so some will sing it without registering the claim.

concerns.title: Two referents in one line
concerns.explanation: The 'He' rescued and the Father doing the rescuing appear together without the distinction being introduced, and the song has spoken of God as one 'He' for two verses beforehand.
concerns.scriptureExcerpt: He is the image of the invisible God… by him all things were created… and in him all things hold together.
concerns.scriptureRationale: Paul makes the same identification, which is why the shift is defensible.

synthesis.summary: A doctrinally dense modern hymn that runs from God's self-existence through creation, providence, the incarnation, a plainly substitutionary cross and Christ's unending reign — never changing subject along the way. Sin is implied rather than named, so it sits best alongside a song of confession. Weighty content, unusually easy to sing.

scriptureReferences.relevance: The opening doctrine: God as source of all, dependent on none.

scriptureReferences.excerpt: Before the mountains were brought forth… from everlasting to everlasting you are God.
scriptureReferences.relevance: The eternality behind calling God uncreated.

scriptureReferences.excerpt: He determines the number of the stars; he gives to all of them their names.
scriptureReferences.relevance: Verse one's move from cosmic scale to personal knowledge.

scriptureReferences.excerpt: Who stretches out the heavens like a curtain, and spreads them like a tent to dwell in.
scriptureReferences.relevance: The biblical precedent for the chandelier image.

scriptureReferences.excerpt: He changes times and seasons; he removes kings and sets up kings.
scriptureReferences.relevance: God's rule over the rise and fall of kingdoms.

scriptureReferences.excerpt: And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory.
scriptureReferences.relevance: The incarnation as the same God entering creation.

scriptureReferences.excerpt: Ransomed… with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot.
scriptureReferences.relevance: The spotless Lamb of the third refrain.

scriptureReferences.excerpt: God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it.
scriptureReferences.relevance: The resurrection as the Father's act, as the hymn has it.

scriptureReferences.relevance: The threefold holy the final verse closes on.
